bullets.text: The FOMC raised the target range by 25 bp to 3.75%-4.0% on September 16, 2026, with no dissents.
CPI rose 3.4% year-over-year in August 2026, up from a prior 3.3%, with a monthly increase of 0.4%.
Core PCE inflation held at 3.3% year-over-year in July 2026, unchanged from the prior reading, with a 3-month annualized pace of 3.0%.
The unemployment rate held at 4.1% in August 2026, unchanged from the prior month.
Nonfarm payrolls rose by 162 thousand in August 2026, up from a prior monthly change of 21 thousand.
Real GDP growth was 1.5% in Q2 2026, down from a prior 2.1%; the 30-year mortgage rate rose 0.08 pp to 7.03% by September 24, 2026.

latest.latest_text: The Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system. Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little. Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.
latest.previous_text: The Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system. Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace despite elevated uncertainty that owes, in part, to the conflict in the Middle East. Productivity growth and capital investment are strong. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little. Inflation remains elevated relative to the Committee's 2 percent goal, in part reflecting supply shocks that have driven price increases in certain sectors, including energy. The Committee will deliver price stability.

read.summary: The Federal Reserve raised the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent. The statement described economic activity as expanding at a solid pace, with strong productivity growth and robust capital investment. Language citing the conflict in the Middle East as a source of uncertainty was removed, replaced with a reference to geopolitical developments and resilient domestic spending. Inflation was described simply as elevated, without the prior reference to supply shocks in specific sectors like energy. The statement added that the rate increase will support a timelier return to the 2 percent inflation goal. The decision was approved by a vote of 12 in favor with none against.
read.rationale: The Committee raised rates by 1/4 percentage point (idx 0) and added language stating that this action will support a timelier return to the 2 percent inflation goal (idx 9), signaling a more assertive stance against inflation. Additionally, the description of inflation was simplified to 'remains elevated' without qualifying supply-shock context (idx 7, idx 8), and productivity/investment language was strengthened to 'strong' and 'robust' (idx 3), reinforcing a more hawkish tone.

minutes.summary: At its July 28–29, 2026 meeting, the FOMC voted 9–3 to hold the federal funds rate target range at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent, with three members (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) preferring a 25 basis point increase. Participants noted the unemployment rate was 4.2 percent in June, largely stable, while economic activity continued expanding at a solid pace, supported by AI-related investment and resilient consumer spending. Total PCE inflation was estimated near 3.7 percent in June, with core PCE near 3.3 percent, both elevated relative to the Committee's 2 percent goal, reflecting tariffs, Middle East conflict-related energy costs, and AI-related demand. Several participants favored raising rates given broad-based price pressures, while most preferred holding steady to gather more information. Participants viewed inflation risks as skewed to the upside and risks to growth and employment as skewed to the downside, citing geopolitical uncertainty and AI-related investment dynamics as key sources of uncertainty.
